notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether num is a perfect number, equal to the sum of its positive proper divisors.
Idea: Sum divisor pairs for i from 1 through floor(sqrt(num)), correct for a square root counted twice, and compare the proper-divisor total with num.
Technique and why it applies: If i divides num, both i and num//i are divisors. The square-root correction prevents counting the same divisor twice, and subtracting num removes the number itself from the total.
Invariant: total accumulates all divisor-pair contributions discovered through the current candidate i, with the square-root duplicate corrected after the loop.
Edge cases: Nonpositive values return False. For num=1, sqrt_num is 1 and total is 1, so total-num is zero and the final comparison returns False.
Complexity: The loop checks O(sqrt(num)) candidates and uses O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the nth Fibonacci number with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1.
Idea: Store the first two Fibonacci values and append each subsequent value as the sum of the previous two.
Technique and why it applies: The recurrence F(i)=F(i-1)+F(i-2) directly constructs the sequence in increasing index order, and fa[n] is the requested term after the loop.
Invariant: Before each iteration i, fa[j] equals the Fibonacci number F(j) for every stored index j.
Edge cases: n=0 returns the first initialized element, and n=1 returns the second without entering the loop. The problem constraints keep n nonnegative.
Complexity: The method performs O(n) additions and stores O(n) values, so time and auxiliary space are both O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the minimum rotations and button presses needed to spell key by aligning its characters on the circular ring.
Idea: Index each character's positions and memoize a recursive cost for a current ring index and key index.
Technique and why it applies: For each next character, the code uses bisect_left to find a position near the current index and compares clockwise/counterclockwise distances to two neighboring occurrences. It adds len(key) for the final button presses.
Invariant: fn(i,j) is intended to represent the minimum rotation cost for key[j:] when the ring pointer starts at i.
Edge cases: The snippet uses cache and bisect_left without importing them, so those names must be supplied externally. It also considers only the nearest occurrence on either side; a farther occurrence could have a cheaper continuation, so this pruning is not generally guaranteed to preserve the optimum.
Complexity: With memoization there are O(|ring|·|key|) states, but each state does constant work after locating candidate occurrences; auxiliary space is O(|ring|·|key|), assuming the missing imports are supplied.

Task and constraints: Spell key by rotating ring characters into position and pressing once per character, minimizing total steps.
Idea: Pre-index all ring positions for each character and use rolling dynamic programming over key prefixes.
Technique and why it applies: For each occurrence of the next key character, the code considers every previously reachable position and adds the shorter clockwise/counterclockwise rotation distance. The best cost for each new position is retained.
Invariant: dp[i%2][j] is the minimum rotation cost after processing i key characters and ending at ring position j; prev lists positions for the previous key character.
Edge cases: Repeated letters are handled by storing every occurrence. The code assumes key characters all occur in ring; otherwise lookup[key[i-1]] is empty and the final minimum may be infinity.
Complexity: If R is ring length and K is key length, the nested transitions take O(K·R²) in the worst case, with O(R) rolling DP space plus O(R) character-position storage.

Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest palindromic subsequence in string s.
Idea: Fill interval DP states in order of increasing substring length.
Technique and why it applies: A one-character interval has length one. Matching endpoints extend an inner palindrome by two; otherwise the best result comes from dropping either endpoint and taking the larger subproblem value.
Invariant: dp[i][j] stores the longest palindromic subsequence length within s[i:j+1] after that interval has been processed.
Edge cases: The method assumes s is nonempty because it returns dp[0][-1]. Two equal adjacent characters give length two; unequal ones use the maximum of the single-character states.
Complexity: There are O(n²) intervals and O(1) work per interval, so time and auxiliary space are both O(n²).

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest palindromic subsequence in s.
Idea: Use two rows of interval DP while processing starting indices from right to left.
Technique and why it applies: Matching endpoints contribute two plus the best inner interval; otherwise the state takes the maximum of dropping the left or right endpoint. Alternating rows retains the next-starting-index results without storing the full table.
Invariant: For the current i, dp[i%2][j] stores the answer for s[i:j+1], while the other row holds results for start index i+1.
Edge cases: A string that is already a palindrome returns its full length immediately. The code assumes nonempty s because it ultimately indexes dp[0][-1].
Complexity: The palindrome check is O(n), and the DP fills O(n²) states in O(n²) time. Two rows each of length n use O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum moves needed to make all washing machines contain the same number of dresses, or return -1 if impossible.
Idea: Check divisibility of the total, compute the average, then use prefix balances and suffix balances to estimate transfers across each machine.
Technique and why it applies: A positive prefix surplus must move right, while a positive suffix surplus must move left. At each machine, the sum of these required flows is a candidate lower bound on simultaneous moves; the maximum across machines is returned.
Invariant: left[i] is the total number of dresses in machines 0 through i, and result stores the largest combined directional flow found.
Edge cases: If the total is not divisible by machine count, the method returns -1. The problem normally gives at least one machine, since the code divides by n.
Complexity: Building the prefix sums and scanning machines take O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the accumulate list.

Task and constraints: Check whether a word follows one of the accepted capitalization patterns: all uppercase, all lowercase, or initial uppercase followed by lowercase letters.
Idea: Handle one-letter words, reject a lowercase first letter followed by uppercase, then infer whether the remaining letters must all be uppercase or lowercase.
Technique and why it applies: The flag u is set only when the first two letters are uppercase. Subsequent characters are rejected if their case conflicts with that inferred pattern.
Invariant: After the first two letters, u indicates whether all remaining characters are required to be uppercase; otherwise they must be lowercase.
Edge cases: Single-character words always return True. The problem uses English letters, so the comparisons against lower() and upper() classify characters as intended.
Complexity: The method scans the word a constant number of times, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a word uses capitalization consistently.
Idea: Return True if the word is all uppercase, all lowercase, or title-cased.
Technique and why it applies: isupper and islower test uniform casing, while istitle accepts an uppercase first letter followed by lowercase letters for ordinary English words.
Invariant: The result is true exactly when one of the three supported capitalization predicates holds.
Edge cases: A one-letter alphabetic word satisfies the appropriate casing predicates. Python's string methods have Unicode-aware behavior, but the problem's inputs are English letters.
Complexity: Each string predicate scans the word, so total time is O(n) and auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest uncommon subsequence between two strings.
Idea: If the strings are identical, no uncommon subsequence exists; otherwise return the length of the longer string.
Technique and why it applies: When a and b differ, the longer entire string cannot be a subsequence of the shorter string. If their lengths tie but they differ, neither can be a subsequence of the other, so the longer length is still valid.
Invariant: The method directly resolves the only two cases: identical strings and unequal strings.
Edge cases: Equal empty strings would return -1; unequal strings return the maximum length. The code does not need to inspect individual characters beyond equality.
Complexity: String equality can take O(min(len(a),len(b))) time in the worst case, with O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the longest subsequence that occurs in one of two strings but not the other.
Idea: Return -1 for identical strings and otherwise return the larger string length.
Technique and why it applies: If strings differ, the longer one itself is a subsequence of itself but cannot be a subsequence of the shorter string. When lengths are equal and strings differ, each whole string is not a subsequence of the other.
Invariant: The equality check distinguishes the no-solution case from all cases where one whole input string is an uncommon subsequence.
Edge cases: The empty-string case follows the same logic: identical empties return -1, while one empty and one nonempty returns the nonempty length.
Complexity: Comparing strings takes O(n) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum length of a string that is not a subsequence of any other string in strs.
Idea: Count duplicate strings, sort unique strings by descending length, and test candidates against all longer or equal-length unique strings.
Technique and why it applies: A duplicated string cannot be uncommon. For a unique candidate, isSubseq checks whether it appears in another string; the first candidate not contained in any prior longer candidate is the longest valid answer.
Invariant: Strings are considered in nonincreasing length order, so the first qualifying candidate has maximum possible length.
Edge cases: The code uses Counter without importing it in the snippet, so Counter must be supplied externally. The helper assumes a is nonempty; the problem's strings are nonempty.
Complexity: If there are U unique strings of maximum length L, pairwise subsequence checks cost O(U²L) in the worst case; counting and sorting add O(N log N). Space is O(total input characters) for counts and sorted keys.

Task and constraints: Return the longest string that is not a subsequence of any other string in the list.
Idea: Sort strings by descending length and test each candidate against every other string of at least that length.
Technique and why it applies: isSubsequence advances through the candidate when matching characters appear in the other string. A candidate qualifies only if no different list position contains it as a subsequence.
Invariant: Before each candidate is tested, all strings of greater length have already been considered; the inner scan checks every possible competing string of equal or greater length.
Edge cases: Duplicate strings disqualify each other because the comparison skips only the same index. Sorting mutates the input list.
Complexity: With N strings of maximum length L, there are O(N²) candidate comparisons and each subsequence check costs O(L), for O(N²L) time and O(1) extra space beyond sorting.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a contiguous subarray of length at least two has a sum divisible by k.
Idea: Track prefix sums modulo k and remember the earliest index at which each remainder occurred.
Technique and why it applies: Equal prefix remainders imply the sum between them is divisible by k. The stored index must be at least two positions behind the current index to satisfy the minimum subarray length.
Invariant: psum maps each seen remainder to its earliest prefix index, and currentSum is the prefix sum through the current element.
Edge cases: This code evaluates currentSum % k without checking whether k is zero, so k=0 causes division by zero if allowed by the problem contract. For positive k, negative prefix sums still produce valid Python remainders.
Complexity: One pass uses O(n) time and O(min(n,k)) map space, with O(n) worst-case auxiliary storage.

Task and constraints: Check whether any contiguous subarray of length at least two has a sum that is a multiple of k.
Idea: Maintain a running prefix sum or remainder and store the earliest index for each remainder.
Technique and why it applies: If two prefix sums have the same remainder modulo k, their difference is divisible by k. Requiring i - lookup[count] > 1 ensures the subarray contains at least two elements.
Invariant: lookup maps each remainder to its first index, preventing later occurrences from replacing an earlier index that gives the longest possible span.
Edge cases: The code handles k=0 by leaving count as the raw prefix sum, so a repeated prefix sum detects a zero-sum subarray. The input values are nonnegative under usual constraints.
Complexity: The method scans nums once, taking O(n) expected time and O(n) auxiliary space for the remainder map.

Task and constraints: Find the longest dictionary word that can be formed by deleting characters from s; break length ties lexicographically.
Idea: Test each dictionary word as a subsequence of s and update the best candidate by length and then lexical order.
Technique and why it applies: j advances only when the current source character matches the next required word character. Reaching the word's length proves it is a subsequence, after which the explicit comparison enforces the tie-break rule.
Invariant: solution is the best valid word found among dictionary entries processed so far.
Edge cases: If no dictionary word is a subsequence, the initialized empty string is returned. The code assumes dictionary words are nonempty because it indexes word[j] inside the source scan.
Complexity: For D dictionary words of maximum length L and source length n, the scan costs O(Dn) time in the worst case. Extra space is O(1) beyond the returned string.

Task and constraints: Select the longest dictionary word that is a subsequence of s, preferring lexicographically smaller words when lengths tie.
Idea: Sort dictionary entries by descending length and ascending lexicographic order, then return the first word that is a subsequence of s.
Technique and why it applies: The ordering places every better-ranked candidate before a worse one. The scan advances a pointer through each candidate only when matching characters are found in s; completing the candidate means it is valid.
Invariant: When a word is returned, all longer words and lexicographically earlier words of equal length have already failed.
Edge cases: If no word can be formed, the method returns an empty string. Sorting mutates the input dictionary list.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(D log D) comparisons with string-comparison costs, and checking candidates costs O(Dn) in the worst case. Auxiliary space is O(1) beyond sorting and the input list.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum length of a contiguous subarray containing equal numbers of zeros and ones.
Idea: Treat zero as -1 and one as +1, then store the first index for each prefix balance.
Technique and why it applies: If the same balance appears twice, the elements between those indices contribute net zero, meaning equal counts of zeros and ones. The earliest index maximizes the span for a repeated balance.
Invariant: total is the balance through the current index, and prefixSum stores the earliest index for each balance encountered.
Edge cases: Initializing balance zero at index -1 allows a valid balanced prefix starting at index zero to be counted. Repeated balances update the maximum without overwriting their first positions.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the prefix map.

Task and constraints: Return the longest contiguous subarray with the same number of zeros and ones.
Idea: Convert each one to +1 and each zero to -1, then use repeated prefix counts to find zero-sum spans.
Technique and why it applies: Equal prefix counts mean the intervening segment has equal zeros and ones. lookup stores the earliest index for each count, and result tracks the longest distance between equal counts.
Invariant: count is the current transformed prefix sum, and lookup maps each seen count to its first index.
Edge cases: The initial entry {0:-1} correctly handles balanced subarrays starting at the beginning. Only the first occurrence of each count is stored, preserving maximum span potential.
Complexity: Each element is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count permutations of 1 through n where the value at each position is divisible by its position or vice versa.
Idea: Backtrack position by position, trying every unused value that satisfies the divisibility rule.
Technique and why it applies: The recursive call fixes the next position only with a valid unused number. Once temp has n values, one complete beautiful arrangement is counted; backtracking removes each choice before trying another.
Invariant: temp contains a valid assignment for positions 1 through len(temp), with no repeated values.
Edge cases: n is positive under the usual constraints. The empty temp at the start means position idx begins at one, and the divisibility checks use that one-based position.
Complexity: The search can explore up to O(n!) permutations, with O(n) recursion depth and O(n) temporary-list storage. Membership checks in temp add O(n) work per candidate in this implementation.
